name: 1793 Chain cent (Flowing Hair, chain reverse)
history: After the 1792 Mint Act, Philadelphia finally had a federal Mint. In March 1793 it delivered its first circulating coins — copper cents. The reverse was a ring of linked chains, meant as unity. Plenty of people didn’t read it that way. Critics saw a bad omen for liberty — “Liberty in chains” — and within months the Mint swapped in a wreath. That short run is why collectors still hunt this one.

name: 1793 Wreath cent
history: The Chain Cent barely cleared the door before the street talked back. Critics said Liberty looked “in a fright,” and that chain reverse wasn’t reading as unity. So the Mint swapped the chain for a wreath — same Philadelphia shop, same year. Flowing Hair Liberty stays on the front; a leafy wreath takes the reverse. One of America’s first circulating redesigns.

name: 1798 Draped bust (heraldic eagle)
composition: Silver, 1485/1664 fine (about .8924), alloy of copper, per the Act of 2 April 1792, §13.
history: In calendar year 1798 the Mint issued 327,536 silver dollars. That is the year's total for all dollars issued, with both the Small Eagle and the Heraldic Eagle reverse and of any date, not a count of Heraldic Eagle coins or of coins dated 1798. Mint Director Elias Boudinot reported that coinage stopped for nearly three months that year, "occasioned by the late calamitous fever, and the decay of some of the machinery." A 1798 Heraldic Eagle dollar shows Liberty engraved by Robert Scot and a Heraldic Eagle reverse adapted from the Great Seal, which replaced the Small Eagle design during 1798. When the change was made, and how the year's total divides between the two reverses, are unconfirmed by official sources.

A 1799 Draped Bust dollar shows Liberty engraved by Robert Scot and a Heraldic Eagle reverse adapted from the Great Seal. name: 1800 Draped Bust / Heraldic Eagle dime
history: In calendar year 1800 the Mint issued 21,760 dimes. That is the year's total of dimes issued, not a count of coins dated 1800. Mint tables list no dimes for calendar 1799. An 1800 dime shows Robert Scot's Draped Bust Liberty and a Heraldic Eagle reverse patterned after the Great Seal. The type has 13 stars, seven left and six right, and no mark of value anywhere on the coin. Collector references list two die varieties, JR-1 and JR-2, and say they make up the entire issue; those names are unconfirmed by official sources. Variety is not assigned to the coin pictured.

name: 1875 twenty-cent piece
composition: 900 parts silver, 100 parts copper (per 1,000 by weight). Applies the standard of the Coinage Act of 1873 (sec. 13). The Act of March 3, 1875 does not itself state this composition; it coins the twenty-cent piece 'conformably in all respects to the coinage act of eighteen hundred and seventy-three'. Director of the Mint, FY1876 report, Table XIV (printed p. 45): 'Weight, 5 grams, or 77.16 grains; fineness, 900.'
history: The twenty-cent piece was authorized by the Act of March 3, 1875. It weighs 5 grams (77.16 grains) and applies the standard of the Coinage Act of 1873: 900 parts silver, 100 parts copper. It was legal tender at face for any amount not exceeding $5 in any one payment. Coinage was prohibited from May 2, 1878.

mintage.label: calendar-year delivery total, business and proof combined. U.S. Mint records show 39,700 twenty-cent pieces delivered at Philadelphia in calendar year 1875. That figure combines circulation and proof strikes. Bureau of the Mint, Domestic and Foreign Coins Manufactured by Mints of the United States (1974 ed.), Table C19, printed p. 36 (FRASER PDF p. 40). Before 21 Nov 1888, coinage was counted by delivery date.

name: 1952 Franklin Half Dollar
history: Mint Director Nellie Tayloe Ross proposed a half dollar honoring Benjamin Franklin and the Liberty Bell. The Treasury announced the design on 7 January 1948 in press service S-589, crediting Chief Engraver John R. Sinnock. Sinnock based Franklin’s profile on his 1933 Mint medal and adapted the Liberty Bell, crack included, from his 1926 Sesquicentennial half dollar. Gilroy Roberts is credited in secondary accounts with finishing the work after Sinnock’s 1947 death (unconfirmed by official sources). The Mint’s fiscal year 1954 annual report, Table 14, lists the type as first coined and first issued in April 1948. The public-sale date of 30 April 1948 is a standard secondary figure (unconfirmed by official sources). The series ran through 1963 and was replaced by the Kennedy half dollar in 1964.

mintage.label: Calendar year 1952, regular design, Philadelphia; proofs not separated (Annual Report of the Director of the Mint, fiscal year 1953, Table 13, p. 22).

diameter_mm.label: unconfirmed by official sources as a millimeter figure; 1.205-inch standard is the underlying statutory size

name: 1797 Draped Bust cent
history: The 1797 Draped Bust cent was a hoard date, now widely distributed among collectors. Some 1797 cents have a strange gripped edge: irregular notches and raised pellets. Its purpose is unknown. Breen guessed it marked a batch of planchets, or came on blanks from outside sources.

name: 1797 Draped Bust half dime (small eagle)
history: In 1797 the half dime came with 13, 15 or 16 stars. The half dime with the small eagle design was only used in 1796 and 1797. Each star once stood for a state. After the 13 originals came Vermont, then Kentucky in 1792, and Tennessee in 1796. The stars got so crowded on the tiny half dime that the Mint went back to 13.

name: 1797 Draped Bust / Small Eagle half dollar
history: Every 1797 half has 15 stars, though 1796 came with 15 or 16. Why the count changed has never been satisfactorily explained. The reverse shows the fraction ½ under a small eagle in an open wreath.

mintage.label: not yet sourced — post/RP cite 3,918 lumped 1796–97 Small Eagle halves; needs Mint/FRASER before fill

varieties.name: 1797 half dollar varieties: O-101 and the rarer O-102, told apart by the reverse lettering relative to the wreath.
PCGS lists die varieties O-101, O-101a and O-102.
This type is the limiting coin for a U.S. silver type set.

name: 1797 Draped Bust / Small Eagle dollar
composition: Silver, 1485/1664 fine (about .8924), alloy of copper, per the Act of 2 April 1792, §13.
history: Bowers believes most coins struck from dies dated 1797 were actually made in early 1798. In 1797 the dollar carried 16 stars. One obverse puts 10 stars left and only six right, an arrangement unique in the dollar series. Yellow fever closed the Mint from late August to late November 1797.

mintage.label: No official mintage for coins dated 1797. The Mint issued 7,776 silver dollars in calendar year 1797, all dates combined.
No official mintage for coins dated 1797 or for any variety.

weight_g.label: 416 grains (about 26.96 g), set by the Act of 2 April 1792, §9.

diameter_mm.label: Not set by law; measurement only. Collector references give about 39–40 mm.

fineness.label: 1485/1664 fine (about .8924), set by the Act of 2 April 1792, §13. Earlier dollars of 1794-95 were struck at .900; the Mint Director ordered the legal standard from late 1795 (report to Congress, 14 Dec 1795).

sources.label: Bureau of the Mint, Domestic and Foreign Coins Manufactured by Mints of the United States (1974), Table C11, p. 16 (PDF page 20) — calendar year 1797, dollars 7,776
Act of 2 April 1792, ch. 16, 1 Stat. 246, §9 (weight: 416 grains standard, 371.25 grains fine) and §13 (fineness 1485/1664; alloy wholly of copper)

Director of the Mint Elias Boudinot, report on the Mint, communicated to the Senate 14 December 1795 (American State Papers, Finance, Vol. 1, No. 84): coins struck before he took office had varied from the legal standard; he ordered that the precise terms of the Act be observed thereafter.

name: 1797 Capped Bust Right / Heraldic Eagle $2.50
composition: Gold, 11/12 fine (0.9167); alloy silver and copper. Legal standard under the Act of 2 April 1792, secs. 9 and 12; not a measured specimen weight.
history: The 1797 $2.50 is one of the rarest of all quarter eagles. The 1797 reverse has sixteen stars above the eagle and sixteen stripes on the shield. That die was evidently made in 1796 and reused, then used again to strike the 1798/7 dime. The two coins' reverse dies were interchangeable.

name: 1 Peso, Victory Series No. 66 Treasury Certificate, Commonwealth of the Philippines, 1944
history: Commonwealth of the Philippines Treasury Certificate, Victory Series No. 66, printed by the United States Bureau of Engraving and Printing in Washington at the request of the Commonwealth Government (U.S. Treasury, War, Navy, and Interior joint statement, Press Service No. 44-9, 16 November 1944). The face carries the series designation 'Victory Series No. 66.' The Commonwealth seal and serial numbers are in blue (the pre-war certificates had used red). The reverse has the word VICTORY overprinted in large open-faced black letters over the colored design. Apolinario Mabini portrait on the face (consistent with specialist listings). Orange back with black VICTORY overprint. Legal authority on the notes, and in Act No. 3058 of 13 June 1922, is an act of the Philippine Legislature approved by the President of the United States. Section 1625 of that act requires the certificates to be printed through the U.S. Secretary of the Treasury and completed at the Bureau of Engraving and Printing at Washington. Section 1626 authorizes issues from one peso to five hundred pesos, payable to the bearer in silver pesos or, as the notes themselves state, in legal-tender currency of the United States of equivalent value. President Sergio Osmeña declared the new Victory Series legal tender in liberated areas by Executive Order No. 25, 18 November 1944, at two Victory pesos to one United States dollar, and kept pre-war Treasury certificates and coins legal tender at par. U.S. TreasuryDirect records that these were obligations of the Philippine Treasury, for use only in the Philippines, then a dependency of the United States, and that the series was later demonetized (500-peso notes by 31 December 1957; remaining denominations exchangeable until 30 July 1967, then considered demonetized). The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas adds that after the Central Bank was created in 1949, Victory Series No. 66 notes were overprinted 'Central Bank of the Philippines' on the reverse and remained legal tender until 30 July 1964. Those 1949 and later overprints are a follow-on variety. This denomination is one of the five named in the 16 November 1944 U.S. joint statement as the new Victory Series then in use. An exact first-issue day (sometimes given in secondary accounts as 20 October 1944, the Leyte landing) is not stated in that joint statement and is unconfirmed by official sources. Fiscal-year sheet deliveries in the Treasury annual reports are not automatically a per-denomination mintage. The 16 Nov 1944 U.S. joint statement says the new series bears the signature of President Sergio Osmeña. Specialist listings commonly pair the 1-peso with Osmeña and Auditor General Jaime Hernandez. The second-signature title (Auditor General versus Treasurer) is unconfirmed by official sources. Roxas–Guevara combinations, if any exist on this denomination, would be after Philippine independence (4 July 1946).

No BEP or official issue record has been found for the first-issue date or the signature combinations. Roxas signatures would be after 4 July 1946.

name: 2-peso silver certificate, Philippine Islands (authorized 1903)
history: Philippine silver certificate authorized by section 8 of the Act of March 2, 1903, 32 Stat. 952. The treasurer of the Philippine Islands could receive deposits of standard silver pesos, in sums of not less than twenty pesos, and issue silver certificates in denominations of not less than two nor more than ten pesos, the deposited coin to be held for payment of the certificates on demand. The certificates were receivable for customs, taxes, and all public dues, and could be counted in a bank’s lawful reserve. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas states that beginning May 1918 treasury certificates replaced the silver-certificate series, and a one-peso note was added at that change. Printer is recorded as BEP on the same statutory pattern later spelled out in Act No. 3058 for treasury certificates (printing through the U.S. Treasury / BEP at Washington). No BEP delivery table for this denomination has been found; print quantity is not yet sourced. Later larger silver-certificate denominations (if any were authorized after 1903) are not listed here because section 8 only names the range two to ten pesos.

name: 1-peso treasury certificate, Philippine Islands / Commonwealth (pre-Victory series, from 1918)
history: Philippine treasury certificate of the series that, according to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, began in May 1918 when treasury certificates replaced silver certificates, and a one-peso note was added. Act No. 3058 of 13 June 1922, §§ 1625–1626, is the later statutory frame: certificates were to be printed through the U.S. Secretary of the Treasury and completed at the Bureau of Engraving and Printing at Washington, in denominations of not less than one peso nor more than five hundred pesos, payable from a 100% Treasury Certificate Fund, and receivable for public dues. This is the pre-Victory type for this denomination (various face series years such as 1918, 1924, 1929, and 1936 are recorded in specialist lists and are unconfirmed by official sources as a complete variety list). It is not the later Victory Series No. 66. Later 1949 Central Bank of the Philippines reverse overprints were issued after independence (the Central Bank was created in 1949) and are not part of this type.

name: Japanese occupation / invasion money, Philippine peso war notes, 1942–1945 (type-series)
history: War notes issued in the Philippines during the Japanese occupation of 1942–1945. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas states that the Japanese Occupation Forces issued war notes in high denominations, with no backup reserves, which Filipinos called “Mickey Mouse” money, and that this period saw the worst inflation in Philippine history. These notes were issued by the Japanese government (occupation authorities), not by the United States. Commonwealth Executive Order No. 25 (18 November 1944) declared Japanese occupation currency not legal tender in liberated areas. This is a type-series entry, not a complete denomination-and-series inventory. Denominations and print totals are not yet sourced from a Japanese ordinance or a BSP denomination table. Later Central Bank or Republic issues are not part of this occupation series.

name: Cebu Currency Committee notes (pre-surrender emergency currency, WWII) — type-level
history: Emergency or guerrilla currency of the Cebu Currency Committee, listed in Republic Act No. 369 (10 June 1949) among the pre-surrender emergency currency recognized for registration and redemption. The statute names the chairman as S. C. Miranda. Republic Act No. 22 (1946) created an Emergency Currency Board to register, deposit, and outlaw unregistered emergency currency, and defined “emergency currency” to include pre-surrender emergency issues, guerrilla issues, and so-called mountain money. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas states that guerrilla or resistance currencies, generally in low denominations, were issued by different provinces and, in some instances, municipalities through their local currency boards. This is a type-level issuer entry. Denominations and print totals are not stated in R.A. 369 (the Act appropriates redemption funds; those sums are not issue or print figures). These notes were issued in the Philippines during the war, generally by Commonwealth, provincial, or guerrilla authorities, not by the United States government.

name: 1 Dollar, Hawaii overprint Silver Certificate, 1942 (Territory of Hawaii emergency issue)
history: Special Currency produced by the Bureau of Engraving and Printing for the Territory of Hawaii in World War II. The BEP History Fact Sheet (April 2013) states that Hawaii Notes were Silver Certificates and Federal Reserve Notes with the word “HAWAII” printed over the face and back, with distinctive brown seals and serial numbers, so that they could be declared valueless if they fell into enemy hands. They were introduced in August 1942 and used in the territory from 1942 to 1944, and also in some Pacific campaigns. The factsheet names the notes used as $1 Silver Certificates and $5, $10, and $20 Federal Reserve Notes. BEP records a combined delivery of 64,138,012 Hawaii Notes (all denominations together). That combined figure is not used as a per-denomination mintage. The FY 1944 Treasury annual report also lists BEP deliveries of silver certificates and Federal Reserve notes overprinted “Hawaii.” These were wartime Special Currency, not ordinary peacetime territorial issues.

name: Yellow Seal silver certificates (North Africa / Sicily special currency, 1942–1944) — type-series
history: Special Currency produced by the BEP: Silver Certificates with a yellow Treasury seal instead of the usual blue seal, so that they could be distinguished and declared valueless if captured. name: Allied Military Lire (Italy) — type-series
mint_facility: Bureau of Engraving and Printing (and contract printers under BEP control)
history: Allied Military Currency described in the BEP History Fact Sheet, Special and Allied Military Currency (April 2013). AMC was produced to supplement local currency for Allied invasion, liberation, or occupation, in the monetary units of the target country. Development and use were directed by officials of the U.S. War, Navy, State, and Treasury Departments and representatives of the British Government. Notes became legitimate currency in an Allied-controlled territory by declaration of the supreme commander of the area. The first AMC. The BEP received formal Treasury authorization in March 1943. Used in Italy; the factsheet also notes Yellow Seal dollars were used in the July 1943 Sicily invasion until Allied Military Lire became available. BEP records a combined delivery of 971,662,000 notes of this currency type. That is a series-level delivery total, not a per-denomination print figure. Denominations are not listed in the factsheet. This is an Allied issue, not solely a United States official currency, even though Treasury authorized BEP production.

name: Military Payment Certificate, Series 461 (type-series)
mint_facility: Bureau of Engraving and Printing (early series also printed under BEP contract by Forbes Lithographic and Tudor Press, Boston, until BEP took over all production in 1964)
history: U.S. Military Payment Certificate Series 461. The BEP produced MPC for the Department of Defense from 1946 to 1973 as controlled scrip for U.S. military and civilian personnel on designated overseas bases. BEP explains the series number: the first two digits are the year the series was printed, the third is the number of the series printed that year — so Series 461 was printed in 1946. The BEP factsheet’s “dates used” column lists 1946–1947 for this series; that area/dates table is sourced on the factsheet to Fred Schwan, Comprehensive Catalog of Military Payment Certificates (2002), and is recorded here as the factsheet’s attribution; that dates-used table is unconfirmed by official sources. Official denominations for this period: 5¢, 10¢, 25¢, 50¢, $1, $5, and $10 (BEP: this was the denomination set for MPC produced 1946–1965; the $20 was added from 1966 on). This is a series-level entry; denomination splits and print totals are not yet sourced. A trial run was carried out in the Pacific Command in July 1946; the Secretary of War approved use in occupied areas of the Pacific, Mediterranean, and Europe in August 1946; Series 461 was issued in September 1946. MPC have not been used by the Department of Defense since 1973; the program was formally canceled in August 2003. 32 C.F.R. § 538.5 (2002) lists Series 461, 471, 472, 481, 521, 541, 591, 611, 641, 651, 661, 681, and 692 as the invalidated issued series. This is official U.S. BEP / Department of Defense scrip.

mint_facility: Bureau of Engraving and Printing (early series also printed under BEP contract by Forbes Lithographic and Tudor Press, Boston, until BEP took over all production in 1964)
history: U.S. Military Payment Certificate Series 611. The BEP produced MPC for the Department of Defense from 1946 to 1973 as controlled scrip for U.S. military and civilian personnel on designated overseas bases. BEP explains the series number: the first two digits are the year the series was printed, the third is the number of the series printed that year — so Series 611 was printed in 1961. The BEP factsheet’s “dates used” column lists 1964–1969 for this series; that area/dates table is sourced on the factsheet to Fred Schwan, Comprehensive Catalog of Military Payment Certificates (2002), and is recorded here as the factsheet’s attribution; that dates-used table is unconfirmed by official sources. Official denominations for this period: 5¢, 10¢, 25¢, 50¢, $1, $5, and $10 (BEP: this was the denomination set for MPC produced 1946–1965; the $20 was added from 1966 on). This is a series-level entry; denomination splits and print totals are not yet sourced. A trial run was carried out in the Pacific Command in July 1946; the Secretary of War approved use in occupied areas of the Pacific, Mediterranean, and Europe in August 1946; Series 461 was issued in September 1946. MPC have not been used by the Department of Defense since 1973; the program was formally canceled in August 2003. 32 C.F.R. § 538.5 (2002) lists Series 461, 471, 472, 481, 521, 541, 591, 611, 641, 651, 661, 681, and 692 as the invalidated issued series. This is official U.S. BEP / Department of Defense scrip.

name: 5¢ AAFES POG gift certificate, 1st printing (ND), plain denomination-only design
composition: Coated disk / cardboard gift certificate (AAFES wording); collectors describe polystyrene or plastic
history: 5-cent AAFES POG gift certificate from the 1st printing, the plain denomination-only design and the only printing without a picture (AFPN 2004: “The first was simply the specific denomination”). Undated (ND) on the piece; issued from late 2001 / November 2001. AAFES POGs are 5¢, 10¢ and 25¢ gift certificates issued as change at AAFES contingency exchanges because the military did not provide coins in the contingency theater, due to the weight of coins and other mission priorities (AAFES News, 7 June 2005). AAFES first issued them in late 2001 (AAFES 07-050), in November 2001 at exchange stores in Afghanistan and elsewhere during Operation Enduring Freedom (AAFES-Europe, quoted by Stars and Stripes, 4 Oct 2003). They are redeemable at any AAFES facility, and at OIF/OEF locations could be exchanged for cash in even-dollar amounts (AAFES 04-007). AAFES began phasing POGs out in Afghanistan in early May 2021 as exchanges there went cashless; POGs remained usable outside Afghanistan (AAFES spokesman Chris Ward, 2021). This was not a worldwide withdrawal.

name: Danish West Indies coinage (pre-1917, before the transfer to the United States) — type-series
history: Pre-U.S. coinage of the Danish West Indies, later the U.S. Virgin Islands. The islands were transferred to the United States under the 1916 convention, with U.S. sovereignty effective 31 March 1917. Issues struck before that date were Danish colonial coins, not United States coins. This is a type-series entry. A full denomination-and-date inventory (commonly described as a mid-19th-century cent/daler decimal coinage and a later franc–bit–daler coinage of the early 1900s, including gold 4- and 10-daler pieces) is unconfirmed here from a Danish mint report or a U.S. Mint or Treasury inventory. After 1917 the islands used United States currency; no separate official U.S.-era Virgin Islands circulating coinage is listed in this entry (the 2009 territory quarter is a separate United States issue).
pre_federal_state: Danish West Indies (later the U.S. Virgin Islands; U.S. sovereignty from 31 March 1917)

sources.label: Convention between the United States and Denmark for the Cession of the Danish West Indies, signed 4 August 1916, ratifications exchanged 17 January 1917, proclaimed 25 January 1917, 39 Stat. 1706. Formal transfer of the islands was 31 March 1917.

name: 1798 Capped Bust Right / Small Eagle $5, BD-1
composition: Standard gold, fineness 11/12 (.9167), per the Act of 2 April 1792
history: The Heraldic Eagle reverse first appeared on United States coinage on the 1796 quarter eagle. On the eagle ($10) it was introduced mid-1797, after Small Eagle $10s of that date. On the half eagle, Heraldic reverses first appear on 1795-dated coins struck c.1797–98. By 1798 the Heraldic reverse was the regular reverse for 1798-dated half eagles; a few 1798-dated coins were still struck from an older Small Eagle reverse (BD-1).

name: 1798 Capped Bust Right / Heraldic Eagle $2.50
composition: Standard gold, fineness 11/12 (.9167), per the Act of 2 April 1792
history: The Heraldic Eagle reverse is adapted from the Great Seal of the United States, but the arrows and olive branch are transposed. On the Great Seal the eagle holds an olive branch in its dexter (its own right) talon and a bundle of arrows in its sinister (its own left). On the coin the arrows are in the dexter talon and the olive branch in the sinister. Dexter is the eagle’s right, which appears on the viewer’s left. 1798 is the only date of the type with 6 stars left and 7 right.

name: 1800 Capped Bust Right / Heraldic Eagle $5
composition: Gold, 11/12 fine (0.9167); alloy silver and copper. Legal standard under the Act of 2 April 1792, secs. 9 and 12; not a measured specimen weight.
history: In calendar year 1800 the Mint issued 11,622 half eagles. That is the year's total of half eagles issued, not a count of coins dated 1800. The figure already on this row is that calendar-year total, with the delivery-date caveat. A collector total of 37,628 is not used; it appears to add the calendar 1800 and 1801 official totals (11,622 + 26,006). An 1800 $5 shows Liberty in a soft cap, engraved by Robert Scot, and a Heraldic Eagle reverse. Collector references (PCGS / Ron Guth) say the Heraldic Eagle reverse first appeared on this denomination in 1797. The Smithsonian record for the 1797 $5 says that coin was probably minted in the following year (1798). The pictured Berlin coin has 13 stars, eight left and five right. Collector references sort 1800 half eagles by a Blunt 1 or Pointed 1 in the date, and note that one variety can show a rim cud over NIT of UNITED. Those names are unconfirmed by official sources. Variety is not assigned to the coin pictured.

name: 1801 Draped Bust large cent
history: In calendar year 1801 the Mint delivered 1,362,837 cents, all dates combined. That is the year's total of cents delivered, not a count of coins dated 1801. The figure and calendar-year label already on this row are kept. An 1801 Draped Bust cent shows Liberty engraved by Robert Scot, in copper, with ONE CENT inside a wreath. Mint tables list no half cents for calendar 1801; the cent was the Mint's only copper coin that year. Collector references also list no half cent dated 1801. This catalog does not add an 1801 half cent row. Collector references describe a 3 Errors reverse (Sheldon 218 and 219) with the fraction 1/000, a one-stem wreath, and IINITED for UNITED; a 1/000 fraction on other dies; and a 1/100 over 1/000 (Sheldon 221). Those names are unconfirmed by official sources. The coin pictured shows IINITED and 1/000; the one-stem wreath is not claimed for this photograph. The ANS record lists Sheldon 219 as a cataloguer attribution, not an official one, and it is not used as the variety assignment here.

name: 1802 Draped Bust large cent
history: In calendar year 1802 the Mint delivered 3,435,100 cents, all dates combined. That is the year's total of cents delivered, not a count of coins dated 1802. The figure and calendar-year label already on this row are kept. An 1802 Draped Bust cent shows Liberty engraved by Robert Scot, in copper, with ONE CENT inside a wreath. Mint tables list 1,362,837 cents in calendar year 1801, about two and a half times fewer. Collector references list two die varieties: a reverse fraction reading 1/000 instead of 1/100, and a Stemless wreath (PCGS No Stems). Those names are unconfirmed by official sources. The coin pictured shows the 1/000 fraction. It has stems under the bow and is not the Stemless wreath variety.

name: 1875 twenty-cent piece, proof
composition: 900 parts silver, 100 parts copper (per 1,000 by weight). Applies the standard of the Coinage Act of 1873 (sec. 13). The Act of March 3, 1875 does not itself state this composition; it coins the twenty-cent piece 'conformably in all respects to the coinage act of eighteen hundred and seventy-three'. Director of the Mint, FY1876 report, Table XIV (printed p. 45): 'Weight, 5 grams, or 77.16 grains; fineness, 900.'
history: The twenty-cent piece was authorized by the Act of March 3, 1875. It weighs 5 grams (77.16 grains) and applies the standard of the Coinage Act of 1873: 900 parts silver, 100 parts copper. It was legal tender at face for any amount not exceeding $5 in any one payment. Coinage was prohibited from May 2, 1878.

name: 1876-CC twenty-cent piece

The Act of March 3, 1875 does not itself state this composition; it coins the twenty-cent piece 'conformably in all respects to the coinage act of eighteen hundred and seventy-three'. Director of the Mint, FY1876 report, Table XIV (printed p. 45): 'Weight, 5 grams, or 77.16 grains; fineness, 900.'
history: The twenty-cent piece was authorized by the Act of March 3, 1875. It weighs 5 grams (77.16 grains) and applies the standard of the Coinage Act of 1873: 900 parts silver, 100 parts copper. name: 1878 twenty-cent piece, proof
composition: 900 parts silver, 100 parts copper (per 1,000 by weight). Applies the standard of the Coinage Act of 1873 (sec. 13). The Act of March 3, 1875 does not itself state this composition; it coins the twenty-cent piece 'conformably in all respects to the coinage act of eighteen hundred and seventy-three'. Director of the Mint, FY1876 report, Table XIV (printed p. 45): 'Weight, 5 grams, or 77.16 grains; fineness, 900.'
history: The twenty-cent piece was authorized by the Act of March 3, 1875. It weighs 5 grams (77.16 grains) and applies the standard of the Coinage Act of 1873: 900 parts silver, 100 parts copper. It was legal tender at face for any amount not exceeding $5 in any one payment. Coinage was prohibited from May 2, 1878.

weight_g.label: 5 grams, or 77.16 grains. Act of March 3, 1875, sec. 1; Director of the Mint, FY1876 report, Table XIV (printed p. 45). Legal standard, not a measured specimen weight.

diameter_mm.label: Numismatic reference (standard trade specification): 22 mm. Not a Mint primary-source specification. PCGS CoinFacts (1875 twenty-cent piece, PCGS #5296) lists the diameter as 22.00 millimeters. Heritage Auctions, sale 1124, lot 2299 (1876-CC twenty-cent piece, cataloged 30 Apr 2009; text confirmed on the 21 Nov 2022 Wayback copy of the public lot page) describes the denomination as having 'a diameter of 22 mm versus 24.3 mm for the quarter'.

fineness.label: 900 parts silver, 100 parts copper (per 1,000 by weight). Applies the standard of the Coinage Act of 1873 (sec. 13). Director of the Mint, FY1876 report, Table XIV (printed p. 45): 'fineness, 900.'

sources.label: Act of March 3, 1875, ch. 143, 18 Stat. 478-479 (govinfo)

Coinage Act of February 12, 1873, ch. 131, sec. 13, 17 Stat. 426. The Act of March 3, 1875 applies this standard ('conformably in all respects to the coinage act of eighteen hundred and seventy-three'); it does not itself state the 900/1000 fineness.

Annual Report of the Director of the Mint, FY1876, Table XIV, printed p. 45 (PDF p. 49): 'Twenty-cent piece. Authorized to be coined, act of March 3, 1875. Weight, 5 grams, or 77.16 grains; fineness, 900.'
Act of May 2, 1878, ch. 79, 20 Stat. 47 (govinfo): coinage of the twenty-cent piece of silver prohibited from May 2, 1878.

name: 1799 Capped Bust Right / Heraldic Eagle $10
composition: Standard gold, fineness 11/12 (.9167), per the Act of 2 April 1792
history: In calendar year 1799 the Mint issued 17,483 eagles. That is the year's total of eagles issued, not a count of coins dated 1799 or of either star variety. Of the $213,285 in gold coin issued that year, eagles made up $174,830; half eagles $37,255; and 480 quarter eagles $1,200. A 1799 $10 shows Liberty in a soft cap, engraved by Robert Scot, and a Heraldic Eagle reverse adapted from the Great Seal. Collectors sort them by Small or Large stars on the obverse; that distinction is a Numismatic reference (standard trade specification), unconfirmed by official sources. Variety is not assigned to the coin pictured.

name: 1800 Draped Bust / Heraldic Eagle dollar
composition: Silver, 1485/1664 fine (about .8924), alloy of copper, per the Act of 2 April 1792, §13
history: In calendar year 1800 the Mint issued 220,920 silver dollars. That is the year's total of dollars issued, not a count of coins dated 1800 or of any variety. In calendar year 1799 the Mint issued 423,515 silver dollars, the only silver denomination listed that year. An 1800 Draped Bust dollar shows Liberty engraved by Robert Scot and a Heraldic Eagle reverse adapted from the Great Seal. The type has 13 stars, seven left and six right; no denomination appears on either face (the value is on the edge). Collector references list several 1800 varieties, including AMERICAI (a die flaw that looks like an I after AMERICA), Dotted Date, 12 Arrows, 10 Arrows, and Wide Date, Low 8. Those names are unconfirmed by official sources. The coin pictured is not AMERICAI and is not assigned a variety; the date is worn but reads 1800.

name: 1802 Draped Bust half cent
history: In calendar year 1802 the Mint issued 14,366 half cents. That is the year's total of half cents issued, not a count of coins dated 1802 or of either reverse variety. Mint tables list 211,530 half cents in calendar year 1800 and none in calendar year 1801. An 1802 half cent shows Draped Bust Liberty engraved by Robert Scot, in copper, with HALF CENT and 1/200 on the reverse. A PCGS CoinFacts figure of 20,266 is stored only as a labeled PCGS CoinFacts note; it is not the official Mint mintage. Collector references describe an 1802/0 overdate with two reverses, C-1 (Reverse of 1800) and C-2, and Ron Guth calls the Reverse of 1800 one of the rarest U.S. half cents; those names are unconfirmed by official sources. PCGS notes that at least one Reverse of 1800 half cent shows an error large cent, cut down, as its planchet; that claim is not generalized to every 1802 half cent. Variety is not assigned to the coin pictured. The photograph (ANS 1906.99.8) shows the date 1802; the overdate is not clearly visible on this image.

name: 1801 Draped Bust / Heraldic Eagle dollar
composition: Silver, 1485/1664 fine (about .8924), alloy of copper, per the Act of 2 April 1792, section 13
history: In calendar year 1801 the Mint issued 54,454 silver dollars. That is the year's total of dollars issued, not a count of coins dated 1801 or of any variety. An 1801 Draped Bust dollar shows Liberty engraved by Robert Scot and a Heraldic Eagle reverse adapted from the Great Seal. Collector references list four 1801-dated varieties, BB-211 (Wide Date, also called B-1) through BB-214 (Close Date). Bowers, writing on PCGS, says only BB-211 could have been struck in calendar year 1801, and that BB-212, BB-213, and BB-214 were struck in 1802 or later; that is a Numismatic reference (standard trade specification), not an official Mint die-date split. The American Numismatic Society lists the pictured coin as Bolender 1, which Bowers equates with BB-211; that attribution is recorded as an ANS and Bowers note, not as a fresh visual call. Proof 1801 dollars are later novodels, not original 1801 coins; they were never part of the 1794-1804 silver-dollar mintages. No firm year for those novodels is stored.

name: 1800 Draped Bust half cent
history: In calendar year 1800 the Mint issued 211,530 half cents. That is the year's total of half cents issued, not a count of coins dated 1800. Mint tables list no half cents in calendar year 1798 and 12,166 half cents in calendar year 1799; those are calendar-year deliveries, not evidence of a 1799-dated half cent. Collector references list no half cents dated 1798 or 1799; the Draped Bust half cent begins in 1800. An 1800 half cent shows Draped Bust Liberty engraved by Robert Scot, in copper, with HALF CENT and the fraction 1/200 on the reverse. Collector references list only one die pairing for the date (Cohen 1 / Gilbert 1800.1); that name is unconfirmed by official sources. Variety is not assigned to the coin pictured.

mintage.label: No official mintage for coins dated 1800, or for the single listed die pairing. The Mint issued 211,530 half cents in calendar year 1800, all dates combined.

name: 2026-P Peace Silver Dollar Reverse Proof (Liberty Bell 250 privy)
history: 2026 Peace Silver Dollar, reverse-proof finish, struck at the Philadelphia Mint with a P mint mark. One-year Semiquincentennial issue with a Liberty Bell privy mark inscribed 250 and the dual date 1776 ~ 2026. On sale 9 Jul 2026. Obverse: Liberty in profile with a radiant crown; inscriptions LIBERTY, IN GOD WE TRVST, and the dual date. Reverse: an eagle at rest holding an olive branch above PEACE; also UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, E PLURIBUS UNUM, and ONE DOLLAR. Design after Anthony de Francisci. Composition 99.9% silver; silver weight 0.859 troy ounce; diameter 1.500 inches (38.10 mm); reeded edge. Mintage limit 250,000 (announced ceiling, not a final mintage).

name: Series 1934 $100,000 Gold Certificate (non-circulating, Wilson portrait)
history: Series 1934 gold certificate with a portrait of Woodrow Wilson, the highest denomination the Bureau of Engraving and Printing ever printed. It was printed from December 18, 1934 through January 9, 1935 and issued only to Federal Reserve Banks against an equal amount of gold held by the Treasury. It was used only for transfers between Federal Reserve Banks and was never in public hands. Private possession is not allowed.

name: Series 1929 $10 National Bank Note, small size Type 2

name: 1946 Iowa Statehood Centennial commemorative half dollar
history: Silver commemorative half dollar marking the 100th anniversary of Iowa statehood, 1846-1946. Obverse: the Old Stone Capitol in Iowa City, with LIBERTY, IN GOD WE TRUST and HALF DOLLAR. Reverse: the Iowa state seal with an eagle, stars above and a banner below, and the motto OUR LIBERTIES WE PRIZE AND OUR RIGHTS WE WILL MAINTAIN. Struck at the Philadelphia Mint. Designer: Adam Pietz.
